subproblem.title: Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the derivative of a map on R^1 equals the squared norm of the derivative along the coordinate line
subproblem.statement: Let l be a natural number, w : R^1 -> R^l an arbitrary map (R^1 = EuclideanSpace R (Fin 1), R^l = EuclideanSpace R (Fin l)), and t a real number. Then hsNormSq(fderiv R w (EuclideanSpace.single 0 t)) = ||deriv (s |-> w(EuclideanSpace.single 0 s)) t||^2. Here fderiv and deriv are Mathlib's derivatives, both 0 at points of non-differentiability. hsNormSq B = sum over i : Fin 1 of ||B(EuclideanSpace.single i 1)||^2.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (ℓ : ℕ) (w : Rn 1 → Rn ℓ) (t : ℝ), hsNormSq (fderiv ℝ w (EuclideanSpace.single (0 : Fin 1) t)) = ‖deriv (fun s : ℝ => w (EuclideanSpace.single (0 : Fin 1) s)) t‖ ^ 2
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Notation. Let e := EuclideanSpace.single 0 1 in R^1, iota(s) := EuclideanSpace.single 0 s, and W := w ∘ iota : R -> R^l.
2. One-term sum. Fin 1 has the single element 0, so for every continuous linear map B : R^1 ->L R^l, hsNormSq B = ∑_{i : Fin 1} ||B(single i 1)||^2 = ||B e||^2 (unfold hsNormSq; Fin.sum_univ_one / simp). Hence the left side equals ||fderiv R w (iota t) e||^2.
3. iota is linear. For every s, iota(s) = s • e: both vectors have unique coordinate s. Hence HasDerivAt iota e t, from (hasDerivAt_id t).smul_const e after rewriting id s • e = iota s.
4. Case 1: w is differentiable at iota t. By the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt applied to hasFDerivAt of w at iota t and step 3), HasDerivAt W (fderiv R w (iota t) e) t. So deriv W t = fderiv R w (iota t) e, and both sides equal ||fderiv R w (iota t) e||^2.
5. Case 2: w is not differentiable at iota t. Then W is not differentiable at t. To see this, let pi : R^1 -> R, pi(z) := z 0, the continuous linear map EuclideanSpace.proj 0; it is differentiable everywhere. We have pi(iota t) = t, and iota(pi z) = z for every z in R^1, since both have the same unique coordinate. If W were differentiable at t = pi(iota t), then W ∘ pi would be differentiable at iota t (DifferentiableAt.comp). But W ∘ pi = w ∘ iota ∘ pi = w, a contradiction. So fderiv R w (iota t) = 0 (fderiv_zero_of_not_differentiableAt) and deriv W t = 0 (deriv_zero_of_not_differentiableAt). By step 2 the left side is ||0 e||^2 = 0, and the right side is ||0||^2 = 0.
6. In both cases the identity holds.
proof_key_steps: hsNormSq B = ||B (single 0 1)||^2 because Fin 1 is a singleton
iota(s) = s • single 0 1 has derivative single 0 1
Differentiable case: chain rule gives deriv (w ∘ iota) t = fderiv w (iota t) (single 0 1)
Non-differentiable case: w = (w ∘ iota) ∘ pi with pi z = z 0, so w ∘ iota is not differentiable at t and both sides vanish

audit.reason: The unconditional identity matches its Lean type. The singleton Hilbert–Schmidt sum and chain rule handle differentiability; composition with the inverse coordinate projection proves nondifferentiability transfers, so both derivatives vanish in the remaining case.
